ⓐ.summary: The decline in US crime is closely related to (reduced) lead exposure.

c1.text: ⓐ The decline in crime in the United States is closely related to lead exposure.

c2.text: US violent and property crime declined sharply from the early 1990s, and the decline continued until 2020.

c3.text: From the end of World War II until the early 1970s, increasing lead emissions from cars were followed by a rise in violent crime.

c4.text: After lead began to be removed from gasoline in the 1970s, violent crime subsequently decreased.

c5.text: Rates of violent and property crime are highest in the late teens to early twenties.

c6.text: For children, unlike adolescents or adults, lead exposure affects brain development and the future potential for criminal behavior, inducing aggression and impulsivity.

c7.text: The effect of childhood lead exposure on crime appears about 20 years later, when the children reach their late teens or early twenties.

h1.text: The average blood lead level of American children aged 1-5 in 2000 had dropped to half the level of 1990.

a.note: Lower childhood lead around 1990-2000 predicts less crime around 2010-2020, which matches the continued decline.

h2.text: The sharp decline in violent crime in the US began in the 1990s rather than the 1970s.

h3.text: The decline in crime is not related to the removal of lead in the 1970s, because the timing does not match.

b.note: Naive timing argument rb1 is undercut by the ~20-year lag c7, so the 1990s start fits ⓐ.

h4.text: Adolescents in the United States who committed crimes had four times the bone lead content of those who did not.

h5.text: Lead exposure is positively correlated with criminal behavior.
